meeting_header:
Date: 2027-06-08
Time: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Sofia Alvarez (Rivermark CTO), Ben Turner (Rivermark ML Eng), Priya Nair (Rivermark SRE)
Recording: Yes
summary: Weekly POC sync focused on latency tuning. Reviewed latest TTFT and streaming test results, discussed sequence length distribution impacts, kernel choices and quantization tradeoffs. Agreed next steps for additional streaming runs, shared kernel/flag recommendations, and to collect Rivermark tail-latency profile for final tuning.
topics: TTFT (time-to-first-token) discrepancies between hosted and dedicated runs
Effect of sequence length distribution on batching and kernel selection
Quantization and kernel choices vs accuracy tradeoffs
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick check - we got 45 minutes, is that still good?
[00:05] Sofia Alvarez: yes that works, thanks.
[00:08] Liam O'Connor: cool, I'll share my screen in a sec, I have the latest TTFT dashboards up.
[00:15] Ben Turner: before we jump in, small note - we saw one run yesterday where the first token took like 280ms and others were 120ms, so curious what changed.
[00:24] Maya Chen: yep that's what we want to dig into, thanks Ben. real quick agenda: TTFT numbers, streaming flush behavior, sequence length distribution effects, kernel picks and quantization, then next steps.
[00:37] Liam O'Connor: ok pulling up the dashboard, so here are the dedicated runs on 2xA100, model variant redwood-7b-q4, default kernel set. you'll notice the median TTFT is around 90ms but the p95 jumps to 240ms.
[00:52] Priya Nair: are these cold starts or warm runs?
[00:56] Liam O'Connor: mix - we have a warmup traffic generator but there are some prefixes that miss the kv cache so it looks like intermittent cache misses. also our streaming test had a flush interval of 200ms which can interact with first-token timing.
[01:12] Ben Turner: hmm we are streaming from the client with small chunks, maybe that combination is bad.
[01:16] Maya Chen: right, two things: TTFT is sensitive to whether the runtime has to rehydrate the KV cache and also to kernel selection for the first decode step. sometimes the first token uses a different matmul path.
[01:29] Sofia Alvarez: can you explain that a bit more? the kernel thing.
[01:31] Liam O'Connor: yeah so some runtimes pick a fused attention kernel for long sequences but revert to a generic kernel for short prefix lengths; that kernel swap can add 30-80ms on that first step. plus if the sequence length changes between encoder and decoder paths we can trigger a JIT or replan.
[01:48] Ben Turner: that sounds like the kernel chooser is based on sequence length heuristics - we have a lot of short queries under 64 tokens though.
[01:55] Liam O'Connor: exactly, so for short queries we recommend forcing the low-latency kernel and disabling a couple heuristic thresholds. I sent a quick patch last night that pins the kernel for decode-1.
[02:06] Maya Chen: note: we'll share the exact flags - it's in the kernel matrix Liam will send after this call.
[02:11] Priya Nair: on streaming, we're seeing partials come in in bursts, sometimes client side aggregates small packets - we do chunked uploads and then flush. could that be affecting TTFT?
[02:21] Liam O'Connor: yes it can. if the client waits to send a full chunk before opening the websocket stream, the server only sees input later and the first token pipeline is delayed. also server side buffering combined with a large flush interval means the server waits to accumulate output. reducing server flush interval helps TTFT but can increase CPU overhead.
[02:38] Ben Turner: tradeoff we understand - we care about low TTFT for interactive traces but want to avoid huge cost spikes.
[02:44] Maya Chen: we can run two modes: low-term TTFT tuning with smaller flush (100ms) and a cost-optimized with 300ms. we'll bench both.
[02:52] Sofia Alvarez: what about sequence length distribution? we did send over a histogram but maybe you haven't used the latest.
[02:57] Ben Turner: we attached a new CSV yesterday showing 75% under 32 tokens, 20% 32-128, 5% over 128.
[03:05] Liam O'Connor: perfect that's consistent with what we saw. for that distribution, batching thresholds should prefer micro-batches and immediate dispatch for the low-latency path. we can disable long-seq batching that groups many short queries.
[03:17] Priya Nair: and quantization? we tested q4 earlier - accuracy drop was minimal but any effect on latency?
[03:24] Liam O'Connor: quantization to q4 reduces memory bandwidth which can improve throughput but sometimes increases decode latency slightly due to dequantization overhead on the critical path. on our hardware, q4 + tuned kernels actually improved median latency and slightly worsened the very first token in some cases.
[03:39] Maya Chen: so practical steps: pin low-latency kernel for decode-1, reduce server flush interval for streaming tests, and tune batching policy to favor immediate dispatch for sequences <64.
[03:51] Ben Turner: can you quantify expected TTFT improvement?
[03:54] Liam O'Connor: ballpark: pin kernel + KV warmup drops median TTFT from 90ms to ~65ms, p95 from 240ms to ~140-160ms. reducing flush to 100ms brings p50 down a further ~10-15ms but increases CPU overhead.
[04:12] Sofia Alvarez: CPU overhead as in cost increase?
[04:15] Liam O'Connor: yes small, maybe 5-10% more CPU on the frontend for high QPS, which may translate to a minor infra cost bump. we'll measure precisely.
[04:24] Maya Chen: for the POC success criteria, remind me - Sofia you said 99th under 300ms and TTFT under 150ms?
[04:32] Sofia Alvarez: yes ideally, for interactive we want 99th under 300ms and cost no more than 20% above our baseline.
[04:39] Ben Turner: baseline being our current on-prem transformer infra.
[04:42] Maya Chen: ok noted. next: we ran an edge-case test yesterday where sequence length jumped mid-request and the runtime recompiled - saw a 400ms spike. that's probably the JIT replan Liam mentioned.
[04:54] Liam O'Connor: right we have a mitigation to pre-allocate decode buffers for common max lengths. that reduces the spike but adds memory.
[05:01] Priya Nair: memory is fine for now but we need the numbers.
[05:05] Liam O'Connor: we'll include memory delta in the kernel matrix doc.
[05:09] Ben Turner: what about VPC/private considerations? if we go private, will KMS calls add TTFT?
[05:15] Maya Chen: good question. KMS on key retrieval is only during startup if using envelope encryption correctly; per-request KMS should be avoidable. network egress from VPC to an external KMS could add latency. recommended pattern: local HSM or a KMS proxy in-region.
[05:29] Sofia Alvarez: we'll have to validate with security but sounds manageable.
[05:33] Liam O'Connor: I'll post an ops note with recommended KMS architecture, including caching the DEK in memory and rotating per policy.
[05:40] Maya Chen: ok wrapping up - quick recap of agreed actions?
[05:44] Sofia Alvarez: go ahead.
[05:46] Maya Chen: Redwood will run two streaming test modes with pinned kernel: low-TTFT (100ms flush) and cost-optimized (300ms flush), share raw logs and consolidated sheet. Liam will send the kernel selection matrix, flags, and expected memory/cpu deltas. Rivermark will share final sequence length histogram and tail-latency SLA targets.
[06:08] Ben Turner: I'll also try to replay our production traffic profile on your test harness, might send over an access token.
[06:15] Maya Chen: perfect. next call same time next week?
[06:18] Sofia Alvarez: yep works. thanks everyone.
[06:21] Liam O'Connor: thanks, we'll follow up in the CRM with attachments.
questions: How much does kernel selection affect TTFT vs KV cache misses?
What is the CPU cost of reducing streaming flush interval to 100ms?
Can KMS be used without per-request network hops in private deployment?
